stem: Meera mixes a small spoonful of curd into a bowl of lukewarm milk and another spoonful into a bowl of cold milk, and leaves both for a few hours. Only the lukewarm milk sets into curd. What best explains this difference?

options.text: Cold milk contains more water than lukewarm milk, so it cannot set.
The microorganisms in the curd starter grow and multiply faster at warm temperatures, turning the milk into curd.
Both bowls form curd equally fast, so the difference is only in how sour they taste.
Warmth kills the microorganisms in the starter, so lukewarm milk sets while cold milk stays liquid.

teacher.key_rationale: Curd formation is caused by Lactobacillus-type microorganisms in the starter fermenting milk sugar to lactic acid; this growth and activity is optimal at lukewarm (moderate warm) temperatures and is greatly slowed in cold milk, so only the lukewarm bowl sets in the same time. A invents a water-content difference, C matches the salient sourness feature while contradicting the given observation, and D reverses the effect of warmth on microbes.
